title: Tenali Raman Tale 100

full_text:
A visiting puritanical ascetic persuaded King Krishnadevaraya that all forms of aromatic herbal pipe smoking (*hookah*) among the courtiers was a sinful distraction from state duties.
Impulsively, the King issued a strict imperial decree:
'Henceforth, any citizen or courtier caught inhaling herbal smoke through a water pipe shall be publicly fined one hundred gold coins and marched through the streets on a backwards donkey!'

The decree caused great grumbling among aged ministers who found comfort in simple evening herbal tobacco after long hours of administration.

Tenali Raman resolved to show the King the absurdity of micromanaging the private habits of peaceful citizens.

The next morning, while King Krishnadevaraya was taking his morning walk through the royal gardens, he smelled a terrible, acrid stench of burning weeds coming from the imperial rose pavilion.
Rushing into the pavilion, the King stood frozen in shock:
Tenali Raman had constructed a massive, six-foot-tall water pipe using an enormous earthenware drainage jug, thirty feet of hollow bamboo tubing, and a smoking furnace of burning dry cow-dung and bitter neem leaves!
Tenali had the bamboo tube in his mouth, puffing furiously, clouds of thick, foul-smelling smoke billowing out across the royal roses!

The King coughed, waved the smoke away, and roared in fury:
'Tenali! Hast thou lost thy mind? Thou art violating my imperial decree inside my own private garden!'

Tenali coughed, bowed with watery eyes, and spoke:
'Maharaj! I am merely obeying your royal command with imperial magnificence!
You decreed that private herbal pipes are forbidden; so I built this public municipal pipe!
I am inhaling the medicinal smoke of cow-dung and neem to purify the palace air of harmful vapors!'

The King stared at the smoking monstrosity, then looked at Tenali’s soot-stained face.
Tenali added gently:
'Jahanpanah, a great Emperor governs the defense of the borders, the justice of the courts, and the feeding of the hungry.
When an Emperor begins regulating whether an old grandfather may smoke a mild herbal pipe on his own veranda at night, he wastes royal authority on trifles and turns his citizens into grumbling lawbreakers.
True temperance is taught through education, not through decrees on water pipes.'

King Krishnadevaraya saw the wisdom behind the smoke.
He laughed heartily, canceled the harsh prohibition, and advised moderation instead, proving that wise governance knows where the law ends and personal freedom begins.
moral: Excessive royal prohibitions that interfere with harmless private customs are cured through satirical demonstration.
